units.t: The Human Body. Episode four.
In this episode: The human brain, How your immune system works and Why we sleep.
Part one. The human brain.
4-kilogram organ with 86 billion nerve cells, running on about the power of a dim light bulb.
Small, thirsty, efficient.
The adult brain weighs about 1.
3 to 1.
4 kilograms, roughly 2% of your body weight, yet it uses about 20% of your energy, even at rest.
That is around 20 watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, which is remarkably efficient compared with computers doing far less.
It is about 75% water and has the consistency of soft tofu, so it floats in protective fluid inside the skull.
It has no pain receptors of its own, which is why some brain surgery can be done while the patient is awake.
Neurons and synapses.
The brain holds roughly 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells.
Neurons send electrical signals along their length.
They then release chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, such as dopamine and serotonin, which cross tiny gaps called synapses to the next cell.
Each neuron can connect with thousands of others, creating an estimated 100 trillion or more connections.
Your thoughts, memories and feelings are patterns of activity across these networks.
Regions and lobes.
The cerebrum is the large, wrinkled outer part.
It handles thinking, language, memory, senses and voluntary movement, and its folds pack more surface area into the skull.
The cerebellum, tucked underneath at the back, fine-tunes balance and learned movements like riding a bike.
The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and runs breathing, heart rate, swallowing and sleep cycles.
Each side of the cerebrum has four lobes.
The frontal lobes handle planning, self-control and personality, and mature last, in the mid-20s.
The parietal lobes process touch and space.
The temporal lobes handle hearing, language and memory, and contain the hippocampus.
The occipital lobes process vision.
Two brain myths.
The brain has two hemispheres joined by a thick bundle of fibres, and each side mostly controls the opposite side of the body.
Some functions lean one way; in most people, language is mainly on the left.
But the idea of 'left-brained' logical people and 'right-brained' creative ones is a myth.
A 2013 study scanning over 1,000 people found no sign that individuals favour one side overall.
Nor do we use only 10% of our brains.
Scans show activity across nearly every region over a day, even in sleep, and damage almost anywhere causes noticeable problems.
An energy-hungry organ that was 90% idle would make no evolutionary sense.
The myth probably grew from misquoted early psychology and survives through movies and self-help marketing.
Rewiring and care.
Your brain physically changes with experience, a property called neuroplasticity.
Learning strengthens or forms connections between neurons, and the adult brain keeps changing throughout life.
London taxi drivers who spent years memorising about 25,000 streets had a larger rear hippocampus than bus drivers on set routes.
After a stroke, other areas can sometimes take over lost functions with rehabilitation.
Brain health is tied to overall health.
Regular exercise increases blood flow to the brain and is one of the best-supported ways to protect thinking skills with age.
Sleep clears waste and consolidates memories.
Social connection and learning are linked to lower dementia risk.
Managing blood pressure, not smoking and limiting alcohol protect your brain too, and a helmet protects it directly.
The key idea: The brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your energy.
Part two. How your immune system works.
Right now, an army of cells is patrolling your body, learning, remembering and fighting invaders you'll never notice.
Layers of defence.
Every day your body meets bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, called pathogens.
Most never make you sick, thanks to your immune system: a network of cells, tissues and organs including the bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils.
It works in layers.
The first layer simply keeps invaders out.
Skin is a tough barrier.
Mucus traps particles in your airways, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it out.
Tears and saliva contain enzymes that break down bacteria, and stomach acid kills many microbes you swallow.
The trillions of friendly bacteria on your skin and in your gut also take up space and resources that harmful microbes would otherwise use.
Fast, then targeted.
If something gets past the barriers, the innate immune system responds within minutes to hours.
White blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages rush in and engulf invaders.
Their chemical signals cause inflammation, the redness, heat, swelling and pain around a cut, which brings more blood and immune cells.
Fever helps too: a higher temperature makes it harder for many pathogens to multiply and speeds up immune reactions.
The adaptive system is slower, taking days, but highly targeted.
B cells make antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto a specific pathogen.
T cells coordinate the response, and killer T cells destroy infected cells directly.
Your body can make enough different antibodies to recognise almost any invader.
Memory and vaccines.
After an infection, some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells.
If the same pathogen returns, they mount a faster, stronger response, often clearing it before you feel sick.
That is why you usually get diseases like chickenpox only once.
Flu and common cold viruses keep changing their outer proteins or come in many varieties, so memory cells miss the new versions.
Vaccines give your immune system a safe preview of a pathogen, using a weakened or inactivated form, a piece of it, or instructions for making a piece, as mRNA vaccines do.
Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people, was declared eradicated in 1980.
When enough people are immune, disease struggles to spread, protecting those who can't be vaccinated: herd immunity.
When it overreacts.
The immune system isn't perfect.
In allergies, it overreacts to harmless substances like pollen, dust mites or certain foods.
Australia has one of the highest rates of food allergy in the world, especially among children.
In autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and coeliac disease, it mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues.
Scientists are still unravelling why, but genetics and environment both play roles.
This is also why you can't 'boost' a healthy immune system into overdrive, and wouldn't want to: an overactive one causes problems of its own.
Supporting your immunity.
You can support your immune system even if you can't boost it.
Regular sleep, physical activity, a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables and fruit, not smoking and moderating alcohol all help it work well.
Staying up to date with vaccinations and washing your hands prevent infections in the first place.
Be sceptical of supplements and products that promise to 'boost immunity'.
For most people, the evidence is weak.
If you get frequent or unusual infections, see a doctor.
The key idea: Your immune system works in layers, and the first is physical barriers such as skin, mucus and stomach acid.
Part three. Why we sleep.
You'll spend about a third of your life asleep.
Here's what your brain is doing, and how to sleep better.
Active, not wasted.
You'll spend about a third of your life asleep, roughly 25 years.
It's not wasted time: sleep is when your body repairs tissue, regulates hormones, supports your immune system and locks in memories.
Every animal studied sleeps, even fruit flies and jellyfish.
Each night runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, moving through light, deep, slow-wave, and REM sleep.
Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night and drives physical recovery.
REM, when most vivid dreams happen, grows longer towards morning.
Your brain is highly active during REM, but most muscles are paralysed so you don't act out your dreams.
Miss sleep and your mood, attention and judgement suffer fast.
Your brain's night shift.
While you sleep, your brain replays the day and strengthens what you learned, moving it into long-term storage.
People remember new facts and skills better after sleeping on them than after the same time awake, and deep and REM sleep both play a part.
Sleep also aids problem-solving: people are more likely to spot hidden patterns after a night's rest.
That's why spaced learning beats an all-night cram.
Sleep may also be cleanup time.
A 2013 study in mice found the brain's "glymphatic" system flushes fluid through brain tissue far more actively during sleep.
This clears waste, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's.
How it applies to humans is still being studied, but it may help explain why chronic poor sleep is linked to cognitive decline.
Your clock and caffeine.
A master clock in your brain, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, runs a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm.
It controls sleepiness, body temperature and hormones.
Light is its main timekeeper: morning daylight starts the day, and as evening falls, melatonin rises to prepare you for sleep.
Bright screens late at night can delay that signal.
Jet lag and shift work are hard because they force you out of sync with this clock.
Meanwhile, a chemical called adenosine builds "sleep pressure" while you're awake.
Caffeine blocks it, masking tiredness.
But caffeine has a half-life of about five hours, so half of a 3 pm coffee is still in you at 8 pm.
Even if you fall asleep, it can reduce deep sleep, so many experts suggest no caffeine within 8 hours of bed.
How much you need.
Most adults need 7 to 9 hours a night, and teenagers need 8 to 10.
Very few people genuinely thrive on less than 6.
Regularly falling short is linked to poorer concentration, mood and immunity, weight gain, and higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.
It's dangerous on the road too: being awake for 17 hours affects driving about as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.
Surveys suggest many Australians regularly don't get enough.
Sleeping better.
Consistency matters most: go to bed and wake at similar times every day, weekends included.
Get daylight in the morning.
Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and use your bed mainly for sleep.
In the hour before bed, dim the lights and follow a wind-down routine.
Limit caffeine later in the day, and alcohol at night, which may help you nod off but fragments sleep later.
If you regularly struggle to sleep or snore heavily, see a doctor: conditions like sleep apnoea are common and treatable.
The key idea: Sleep is active maintenance, running in ~90-minute cycles of light, deep and REM sleep.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What makes the brain's energy use remarkable?
Answer. It uses about 20% of the body's energy at about 2% of its weight.
Question two. Which of these is part of the body's first line of defence?
Answer. Skin, mucus and stomach acid.
Question three. Why isn't sleep "wasted time"?
Answer. It's when your body repairs, regulates hormones and locks in memories.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
